_comment: OPS-DEPLOY-INTERLOCK-CRON-DEFER-W1, made PER-HOST by OPS-HOST-AUTO-REBOOT-W1 — the DECLARED set of scheduled work a HOST-LEVEL DISRUPTION can decapitate. Read by ops/scripts/deploy-cron-interlock.sh (signal-1 deploys) and ops/monitoring/kernel-auto-reboot.sh (aoe-1 reboots), asserted by scripts/check-cron-interlock-coverage.mjs. THE CLASSIFICATION IS THE DELIVERABLE; the dispatch code around it is small. EVERY ROW DECLARES ITS `host`, and `_enumeration` / `_containers` / `_residual_no_safe_kill` are keyed by host — because the DISRUPTION EVENT differs per host and so does the enumeration that finds it. signal-1's event is `docker compose up --force-recreate`, which kills `docker exec`s; aoe-1's is a REBOOT, which is strictly larger — it stops every container, every host process and every in-flight Prefect run, so a `docker exec` grep is the WRONG INSTRUMENT there and would have produced a 1-row population and a structurally vacuous gate on the only host that reboots. Placement is DERIVED, not taste: check-declaration-coverage.mjs pins CONSUMER_DIRS = ['ops/monitoring','ops/cron'], so a declaration read only from ops/scripts/ has zero readers there and would sit half-declared; and it needs no sync because deploy.yml runs `git reset --hard origin/main` BEFORE it invokes the interlock, so this file is always current at the only moment it is ever read. (monitoring-inventory-reconcile.py's ORPHAN scan is scoped to MONITORING_DIR=/opt/algovault-monitoring and never sees ops/scripts/ — the CONSUMER_DIRS leg is the load-bearing one.)

_classes.safe-to-kill: Atomic-replace publish, checkpoint-resumable, or idempotent on next fire. The deploy does NOTHING. The row exists so a future reader sees the job was CONSIDERED, not missed.
_classes.preempt-and-catchup: Killing loses work that a bounded catch-up can repair. SIGTERM, wait up to the derived budget for a checkpoint, then launch an SLO-gated catch-up detached.
_classes.no-safe-kill: Neither atomic nor repairable. Bounded wait, then PROCEED ANYWAY with a loud DEFERRED record. A deploy must never hang on a batch job.
_classes._indeterminate: A row whose `reason` is missing or empty is INDETERMINATE, never a silent safe-to-kill. Same convention as schedule-boundary-rule.json's exemptions.

signal-1.command: crontab -l | grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)'   # then resolve each entry to its script and grep that script for a command-position `docker exec`
signal-1.note: Rows are keyed by PROCESS PATTERN, not by cron line: the interlock matches patterns, and one pattern (seed-signals.js) covers 28 cron lines. `cron_lines` on each row records the fan-out so the enumeration stays recoverable. The prior enumeration measured 91 active lines (OPS-HOST-KERNEL-REBOOT-W2) and 75 before that (W1) — re-derive, never inherit.

aoe-1.command: crontab -l | grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)'   # 7 lines   &&   docker exec aoe-prefect-server python -c '<read_deployments + schedules>'   # 11 deployments   &&   docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'   # 8 containers   — the UNION is the population, because a reboot stops all three. Deliberately NOT signal-1's `grep docker exec`: aoe-1 has ZERO direct docker-exec cron lines and exactly one indirect, so that command measures almost nothing here.
aoe-1.note: Prefect INTERVAL schedules are derived from their anchor, never assumed: retune_nightly 86400s @ 2026-05-29T07:04:40Z, w2_gate_watcher 3600s and w3_gate_watcher 900s @ 07:04:41Z. Cron+Prefect union leaves :05-:12 as the longest contiguous clear run (8 min) — re-derived 2026-08-29, matching the W2/W3 hand-measured window rather than inheriting it.

signal-1.evidence: deploy.yml runs `docker compose up -d --build --force-recreate` in /opt/crypto-quant-signal-mcp; docker-compose.yml declares services mcp-server, facilitator, postgres. The plausible-ce-* containers are a SEPARATE compose project and are not touched.
signal-1.note: A `docker exec` into ANY of the three dies at that moment. `docker exec` into a non-signal-mcp container, and any host process, is out of scope by construction — see `exclusions`.

aoe-1.restart_policy: unless-stopped on ALL EIGHT — measured 2026-08-29 via `docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy.Name}}'`, not inherited from the boot contract, which names only the 4 must-survive.
aoe-1.evidence: Last boot 2026-08-27T15:02:01Z (`uptime -s`): 6 of 8 containers reached StartedAt at boot+19s with RestartCount=0. The two later StartedAt values are unrelated to the boot cycle — aoe-pg-tunnel reconnects on peer-side Postgres bounces (RestartCount 7) and promotion-scanner restarted ~19h in.
aoe-1.note: A reboot stops all eight and `unless-stopped` brings all eight back. The supervisor has never been needed across three hand-run reboot cycles (W1/W2/W3).

rows.reason: Checkpoints at a venue/group boundary and resumes from DB state, so a truncated run is safe — but 10 of 32 nightly runs (31.2%, 60d window, measured 2026-08-22) ended early, 10 of 10 attributed to a deploy, and the resulting lag can push a major venue past its 24h SLO. Preemption is kept because it costs zero deploy latency; the harm is REPAIRED afterwards by an SLO-gated catch-up rather than prevented.

Its PARENT nightly-carry-labeler.js is deliberately NOT the pattern — the child is the resumable half, and the parent dies with the container regardless.

rows.reason: It sends an on-chain Base-mainnet `publishRoot` transaction and THEN writes the batch row + per-signal proofs to Postgres. Measured 2026-08-29: tx confirmed 00:05:04.169Z, batch complete 00:05:07.639Z — a ~3.5s window in which a recreate leaves a Merkle root committed on chain with no database record of it. Re-running does not repair that: getNextBatchId() mints a NEW batch id, so the orphaned root is permanent. Not atomic, not resumable, not idempotent — the only row in this registry that is genuinely none of the three.
rows.runtime_instrument: /var/log/merkle-publish.log — ISO-stamped lines grouped into runs on a 600s gap; max span over n=7 runs, read 2026-08-29
rows.notes: THIS IS THE ROW THAT KEEPS THE 18:00-02:59 UTC WINDOW ALIVE AS A DECLARED CONTROL. It fires at 00:05 UTC, inside that window, which is very likely what the folklore was protecting without anyone having written it down. The whole job is ~7s, so a 120s bounded wait covers it comfortably — the deploy is delayed by at most one job length and then PROCEEDS regardless.

rows.reason: A 7h+ weekly LLM probe sweep with no checkpoint and no resume: a kill loses the whole week's GEO measurement, the next fire is 7 days away, and re-running costs real LLM spend for data that is dated to its run week. No bounded catch-up can repair it, and no bounded wait can outlast it — so the honest ruling is a loud DEFERRED and a deploy that proceeds anyway.
rows.runtime_instrument: /var/log/geo-weekly-cron.log mtime 2026-08-24T08:12:43Z minus its scheduled fire Mon 01:00:00Z = 26,363s; n=1 (the log carries no per-line timestamps, so only the most recent fire is derivable). Lower bound, not an average.
rows.notes: Its own log tail carries `[pg-pool] idle client error (recovering): terminating connection due to administrator command` — the signature of a Postgres bounce hitting it mid-run. It RECOVERED from that one and kept extracting, so the pool is resilient to a postgres recreate; the exposure is the mcp-server recreate, which kills the `docker exec` itself with nothing to recover. Also fires inside the 18:00-02:59 window.

rows.reason: Idempotent on next fire, and killing it is if anything corrective: every cron line is `flock -n`-guarded, so while one instance is stuck the next fire SKIPS rather than queues. A kill releases the lock and the following fire re-derives from live venue state. Nothing is lost that the next sweep does not recompute.

rows.notes: The single longest-lived non-labeler process measured on the box (2h19m). It is on this list because its LIFETIME makes a deploy collision near-certain, not because the collision is harmful.

rows.reason: Idempotent on next fire at a 3-minute cadence and `flock -n`-guarded. It backfills outcomes for signals that do not yet have them, driven entirely by DB state, so a truncated run leaves exactly the same work queued for the next fire ~3 minutes later.

rows.notes: Runs far longer (13m) than its 3-minute cadence, so an instance is alive most of the time and a deploy nearly always kills one. Harmless by construction, and recorded so that is a finding rather than an assumption.

rows.reason: Backlog-driven and budgeted: it labels UNLABELED decisions from DB state under `--max-decisions 4000 --time-budget-min 90`, so it already terminates mid-backlog by design every night. A deploy-induced kill is indistinguishable from hitting the budget, and the remainder is picked up by the next nightly. Its `--check` pre-pass records the backlog size, so a growing queue is visible rather than silent.

rows.reason: Every deployment is a short, DB-state-driven tick that is idempotent on its next fire: the gate watchers re-evaluate live state, promote/advance/regression re-derive from the same rows, and the digests re-render. A killed run is re-scheduled by Prefect on the next tick with nothing to repair. The longest observed run is chaos_nightly at 60.3s — and that one exists to verify recovery, so a reboot during it is re-verified the following night. regime_burst carries no schedule at all (event-triggered), so a reboot cannot interrupt a scheduled fire of it.

exclusions.what: The 42 active cron lines on signal-1 that never reach a crypto-quant-signal-mcp-* container. 100 active lines, 46 with a direct `docker exec`, 12 more reaching one through a host script — 58 covered by `rows`, 42 excluded here.
exclusions.reason: `docker compose up -d --build --force-recreate` recreates only the three services in /opt/crypto-quant-signal-mcp/docker-compose.yml. A cron that runs as a host process, or execs into a container belonging to another compose project, is not reachable by this deploy at all — there is nothing for an interlock to protect. Excluded by construction, not by judgement.
exclusions.re_derivation_command: crontab -l | grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' | grep -v 'docker exec'   # then, for each resolved script path, `grep -E '(^|[;&|]|\$\(|\bexec[[:space:]])[[:space:]]*docker[[:space:]]+exec' <script>` and confirm it is empty

exclusions.reason: OUT OF SCOPE FOR THIS DEPLOY, settled by probe rather than by assumption. It belongs to the algovault-bot repo (absent from this one), and it runs a HOST process — `/opt/algovault-bot/.venv/bin/python scripts/entitlement-drain.py` — with zero `docker exec` anywhere in it. `docker compose up --force-recreate` on the signal-mcp stack cannot touch it.
exclusions.separate_finding: Its SCHEDULE is a different problem and is deliberately NOT fixed here: those ten minutes occupy every canonical off-boundary slot in the hour, which is why signal-1 has only :09 and :39 free and why OPS-HOST-AUTO-REBOOT-W1 faces a 2-minute target. Filed as OPS-BOT-CRON-SCHEDULE-GREED-W1; it is a bot-repo change and cannot ship from a signal-mcp wave. Note also that the script's own header docstring claims `*/5 * * * *`, which the live crontab contradicts — the docstring is stale and belongs to the same follow-up.

exclusions.reason: Both contain the literal string `docker exec`, and neither invokes it. One occurrence is a `#` comment recording a RETIRED implementation; the other sits inside an alert-body heredoc ('... host dist/ unusable AND docker exec failed ...'). A mention is not an invocation — the same rule check-canaries-wired.mjs already carries for comments and check-test-budget.mjs carries for string literals. scripts/check-cron-interlock-coverage.mjs therefore matches `docker exec` only in COMMAND POSITION, after stripping comments.
exclusions.re_derivation_command: sed -E 's/(^|[[:space:]])#.*$/\1/' ops/cron/<f>.sh | grep -cE '(^|[;&|]|\$\(|\bexec[[:space:]])[[:space:]]*(sudo[[:space:]]+)?docker[[:space:]]+exec\b'   # expect 0 for these two, 1..2 for the three real ones

signal-1.ruling: The 18:00-02:59 UTC deploy-free window is NOT retired. It is now a DECLARED control with two named rows justifying it, both of which fire inside it (00:05 and Mon 01:00). What changes is that it stops being folklore carried by an agent-side memory file — a third rule source in an estate that declares two — and becomes data these rows own. OPS-HOST-AUTO-REBOOT-W1 should read this block, not the memory file.
signal-1.retire_when: publish-merkle-batch writes its batch row in the same transaction boundary as (or before) its on-chain send, and geo-weekly-cron gains a checkpoint. Neither is in scope here.

aoe-1.ruling: ZERO — and that is the measured reason aoe-1 is the right host to automate FIRST, not a gap in the enumeration. Every candidate is atomic-on-restart (8 containers, unless-stopped), idempotent on next fire (11 Prefect schedules, max 60.3s), or a read-only probe (7 crons, max 43s). Nothing on aoe-1 writes on-chain, publishes externally, or holds an unrepairable critical section — unlike signal-1, whose two no-safe-kill rows are exactly what keeps the 18:00-02:59 UTC deploy-free window alive.
aoe-1.gate_is_not_vacuous: kernel-auto-reboot.sh's third gate can therefore never ABORT today. That is a REPORTED pass, never a silent one: the gate prints the aoe-1 row count it evaluated, so a zero that means 'nothing is unsafe' stays distinguishable from a zero that means 'the filter is broken'. Its value is forward-looking — the day a no-safe-kill job lands on aoe-1, the reboot starts deferring without anyone remembering to wire it.

_hosts.signal-1: 204.168.185.24 — the revenue host. Disruption event: `docker compose up -d --build --force-recreate`.
_hosts.aoe-1: 178.104.200.44 — the AOE tuner. Disruption event: an unattended kernel REBOOT (OPS-HOST-AUTO-REBOOT-W1).
_hosts._why_per_host: A row consulted for the wrong host is a guard reading a green light for a road it is not on. Every consumer MUST filter rows by the host it is acting on, resolved through the estate's identity chain (MONITORING_HOST_LABELS -> /etc/algovault-host-label -> REFUSE), never a default.
